extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics/introduction to proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Determine and prove whether a given binary relation has properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), understand equivalence relations and equivalence classes, and treat functions as special relations (domain/codomain/range, equality, representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive property
rubrics_metrics.description: For every x in A, xRx (each element relates to itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove reflexivity use a direct argument: take an arbitrary x ∈ A and show xRx. Example: for congruence mod n, n|(x-x)=0 so x = x (mod n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric property
rubrics_metrics.description: For all x,y ∈ A, if xRy then yRx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by direct implication: assume xRy, manipulate the defining relation to show yRx. Example: for congruence mod n, if n|(x-y) then n|(y-x) by multiplying by −1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive property
rubrics_metrics.description: For all x,y,z ∈ A, if xRy and yRz then xRz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine the hypotheses algebraically or logically to derive xRz. Example: for congruence mod n, x-y = na and y-z = nb ⇒ x-z = n(a−b), so n|(x-z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (Definition 11.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show all three properties hold. Equivalence relations often express a notion of 'sameness' (equality, same parity, same sign, same degree for polynomials). Once established, many structural consequences (equivalence classes, partitions) follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class [a]
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A and a ∈ A, the equivalence class containing a is [a] = { x ∈ A : xRa } (Definition 11.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use [a] to collect all elements equivalent to a. Key facts: Theorem 11.1 ([a] = [b] iff aRb) and examples (e.g. congruence classes mod n: [0],[1],...,[n−1]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition of a set
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition of A is a set of subsets whose union equals A and whose pairwise intersections are empty (Definition 11.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence classes of an equivalence relation form a partition (Theorem 11.2): show union of classes equals A and distinct classes are disjoint. Conversely, any partition yields an equivalence relation (xRy iff x and y lie in same piece).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation from A to B
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation from A to B is a subset R ⊂ A × B; often abbreviated xRy for (x,y) ∈ R (Definition 11.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat relations as sets of ordered pairs. For relations from A to B draw diagrams with labeled nodes for A and B and arrows from x to y when xRy. This viewpoint generalizes relations beyond comparisons within a single set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a special relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f from A to B is a relation f ⊂ A × B such that for each a ∈ A the relation f contains exactly one ordered pair of the form (a,b); denote (a,b) ∈ f by f(a)=b (Definition 12.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify uniqueness of output for each input (vertical line test in usual graphs). Representations: graph (subset of A×B), arrow diagrams, formulas. Examples illustrate domain/codomain/range distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain, range
rubrics_metrics.description: For a function f : A → B, domain = A, codomain = B, range = { b : (a,b) ∈ f } = { f(a) : a ∈ A } (Definition 12.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify each explicitly when given f. Note the range is a subset of the codomain; they need not coincide (example: f: Z→N, f(n)=|n|+2 has range {2,3,4,...} ⊂ N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two functions f : A → B and g : C → D are equal iff A = C, B = D and f(x) = g(x) for every x ∈ A (Definition 12.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality requires same domain and same codomain as well as identical outputs on every input. Two rules that give the same outputs but different codomains are not equal as functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integers modulo n (Z_n) and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n ∈ N the equivalence classes of ≡ (mod n) are [0],[1],...,[n−1]; Z_n = { [0],[1],...,[n−1] } with operations [a]+[b]=[a+b] and [a]·[b]=[ab] (Definition 11.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret elements of Z_n as equivalence classes (not numbers). Use addition and multiplication tables (examples given for Z_5). Recognize algebraic laws (commutativity, distributivity) hold for these class-operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness of operations on equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations on equivalence classes must be independent of representative choices: if [a]=[a'] and [b]=[b'] then [ab]=[a'b'] (page proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove well-definedness by using the defining divisibility relations (e.g. a≡a' (mod n) ⇒ n|(a−a'), similarly for b, then expand ab − a'b' and factor out n to conclude n|(ab−a'b')). Similar argument for addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 11.1: [a] = [b] iff aRb
rubrics_metrics.description: For an equivalence relation R on A and a,b ∈ A, [a] = [b] if and only if aRb (Theorem 11.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflexivity to show a ∈ [a]; equality of classes gives a ∈ [b] so aRb. For the converse show inclusion both ways: if aRb then any x∈[a] gives xRa and aRb ⇒ xRb (transitivity), hence x∈[b], and similarly the other inclusion using symmetry and transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 11.2: equivalence classes form a partition
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is an equivalence relation on A then { [a] : a ∈ A } is a partition of A (Theorem 11.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove union of all [a] equals A (every x ∈ A lies in [x]). Prove distinct classes are disjoint: if [a] ∩ [b] ≠ ∅ then pick c in intersection to deduce aRb and hence [a]=[b] (contrapositive shows disjointness when classes differ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical/diagrammatic representation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite relations/functions are often visualized with node-and-arrow diagrams or Cartesian-grid graphs; infinite relations may be impractical to draw (e.g. equality on R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For functions draw arrows from inputs to outputs or plot graphs when domain/codomain are numeric; for relations on different sets draw A and B side-by-side and arrows from elements of A to elements of B. Use diagrams to check properties in finite examples.
